title: Berkshire 1997 letter: waiting for the fat pitch, float, and why cash beats stock in acquisitions
summary: Buffett explains why Berkshire's 34.1% gain was merely a "quack" in a bull market, how size erodes returns, and why savers should welcome falling prices. He details insurance float economics, super-cat discipline, GEICO's low-cost model, and confesses that stock-funded mergers have cost shareholders money.

principles.text: Judge results against peers and the index, not against a rising tide; bull markets flatter everyone.
principles.quote: In a bull market, one must avoid the error of the preening duck that quacks boastfully after a torrential rainstorm, thinking that its paddling skills have caused it to rise in the world.

principles.text: Wait for the fat pitch: don't swing at mediocre opportunities just to be active.
principles.quote: waiting for the fat pitch would mean a trip to the Hall of Fame; swinging indiscriminately would mean a ticket to the minors.

principles.text: Size is the enemy of returns; high past performance came from being small, not smarter.
principles.quote: We weren't smarter then, just smaller. At our present size, any performance superiority we achieve will be minor.

principles.text: Net savers should want lower stock prices, since they are buyers of the 'hamburgers'.
principles.quote: Prospective purchasers should much prefer sinking prices.

principles.text: Float is only valuable if its cost is below the market cost of money; a negative cost means you are paid to hold it.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Paying cash rather than issuing stock protects owners when your existing businesses are better than what you'd buy.
principles.quote: Because our roster is filled with .380 hitters, we have tried to pay cash for acquisitions, and here our record has been far better.
